processing: Made as steamed sencha, and bred with semi-fermented tea in mind too; researchers have tested light withering, pan-firing and black tea processing to bring out its aroma.
harvest_season: Spring first flush; season details vary by grower.
appearance_dry: As sencha, dark green rolled needles, as is typical of the style.
appearance_liquor: As sencha, clear yellow-green, as is typical of the style.
appearance_wet: Soft green leaf, as is typical of steamed sencha.
taste_profile: Strikingly aromatic for a sencha, with fruity and floral notes over a green tea base.

brewing.notes: Use a warmed cup and smell it as you drink, since aroma is the point. Withered versions can take a little more heat.

vintage_note: As usual for Japanese green tea, it is sold as the current spring harvest and best drunk within about a year. It is a specialist name, usually a small single-cultivar lot, and withered or semi-oxidised versions are sold under the producer's own description.
description:
Soufuu is the Japanese cultivar to try if you think sencha only tastes of grass. In comparison with Yabukita, its aroma comes out noticeably more fruity and floral.

It was bred for semi-fermented tea as well as green tea, and that shows in how people experiment with it. Researchers have worked with light withering to lift the aroma, and have tried it pan-fired and as black tea.

The scent is shaped by compounds including linalool, β-damascenone and methyl jasmonate. In the cup that reads as fruit and flowers above a normal green tea body. Brew at moderate heat, and focus on the fragrance rather than strength.

It also contains about 2.5 times as many quercetin glycosides as Yabukita, a figure shared with Saemidori. If you enjoy it, look for a withered Japanese green tea next to see how far this kind of aroma can go.
history: Soufuu is a product of Japanese public tea breeding, developed for both green and semi-fermented tea. Research on its aroma and processing appears in the bulletins of the national vegetable and tea institute and in the Japanese tea science journal, and NARO has also published on its flavonol content.
